extracted.intended_audience: general literate public; readers of The Spectator (early-18th-century gentlemen and ladies interested in morals, taste, and polite literature)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing short moral/reflective prose (fables, framed anecdotes, and seasonal essays) that instructs, satirizes, or inspires gratitude; emphasizes moralization of observation and use of character-detail and irony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable should expose human follies and carry a moral
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding the Levity of this Fable, the Moral of it very well deserves our Attention... The Vanity of Mens Wishes, which are the natural Prayers of the Mind, ... are sufficiently exposed by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the fable form to make a pointed moral: show absurd or extravagant human desires (illustrated by the petitions presented to Jupiter) so that the reader sees the folly. The author explicitly aligns this tradition with Socrates, Plato, Juvenal, and Persius as exemplary moral satirists. (Context: the trap-door scene with petitions to Jupiter; the concluding sentence urging attention to the moral.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use set forms / restraint to prevent extravagant expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Among other Reasons for set Forms of Prayer, I have often thought it a very good one, that by this means the Folly and Extravagance of Mens Desires may be kept within due Bounds, and not break out in absurd and ridiculous Petitions on so great and solemn an Occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates formalizing or restraining expression (here applied to prayer) so that private excesses or absurdities are curbed; in a literary sense this recommends structural or formal devices to keep sentiment and rhetoric from running into absurdity. (Statement appears as an applied moral lesson drawn from the fable.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame narrative or dream as a vehicle for satire/character portrait
rubrics_metrics.description: I was lately at a Tea-Table... This whimsical Thought worked so much upon my Fancy the whole Evening, that it produced [a very odd Dream.] Methought, that as I stood before my Glass, the Image of a Youth ... appeared in it; who with a small shrill Voice spoke in the following manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with a familiar social scene and introduce a dream or vision as a plausible framing device to deliver satire or character critique. Personify an object (the looking‑glass) to speak truthfully and ironically; use first-person framing to lend immediacy and amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict characters by concrete, telling details to reveal vanity and self-regard
rubrics_metrics.description: I was the Confident and Darling of all the Fair; ... Flavia colour'd her Hair before me, Celia shew'd me her Teeth, Panthea heaved her Bosom, Cleora brandished her Diamonds; I have seen Cloe's Foot, and tied artificially the Garters of Rhodope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveal characters’ priorities and vanities through small, specific actions and objects (hair, teeth, garters, jewels, gestures). Let these concrete particulars demonstrate self-love and social affectation rather than explicit authorial comment—the particulars supply irony and ethical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: When writing on nature/seasonal pleasure, moralize it into a virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: I would have my Readers endeavour to moralize this natural Pleasure of the Soul, and to improve this vernal Delight ... into a Christian Virtue. When we find our selves inspired with this pleasing Instinct ... let us consider to whom we stand indebted for all these Entertainments of Sense ... A grateful Reflection ... sanctifies it in the Soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform descriptive writing about nature into moral or religious reflection: encourage readers to convert transient delight in spring/nature into gratitude, praise, and habitual virtue. Cite poets and scripture (Milton, the Psalmist, the Apostle) to model how natural description can prepare the mind for thanksgiving and devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use natural philosophy (causal/teleological explanation) to deepen nature writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural Philosophy quickens this Taste of the Creation, and renders it not only pleasing to the Imagination, but to the Understanding. It does not rest in the Murmur of Brooks ... but considers the several Ends of Providence which are served by them, and the Wonders of Divine Wisdom which appear in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mere picturesque description: explicate the purposes and order behind natural phenomena (Providence, teleology) so that delight is joined to rational admiration. This method heightens sensory pleasure and makes it serviceable to intellectual and devotional ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ irony and exaggerated petitions to satirize societal follies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Philosopher seeing a great Cloud ... enquired of Jupiter what it meant. This, says Jupiter, is the Smoke of a whole Hecatomb that is offered me by the General of an Army ... But hark, says Jupiter, there is a Voice I never heard but in time of danger; tis a Rogue that is shipwreck'd ... a Pious Lady, desiring Jupiter that she might appear amiable and charming ... the Isle of Paphos ... that whimsical Tribe of Mortals who are called Lovers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To expose follies, assemble absurd requests or speeches (here the catalogue of petitions to Jupiter) and let the divine/superior speaker respond with dry, ironic commentary. The catalogue form, absurd escalation, and juxtaposition of trivial and grave petitions produce satirical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: On wit (punning): allow diversion but beware excess and shallowness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Monopoly of Punns ... The way this Gentleman's Passion for the Brunette has suggested ... Punning ... may be as instrumental in diverting us from any innovating Schemes and Hypothesis in Wit, as dwelling upon honest Orthodox Logic would be in securing us from Heresie in Religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat light verbal wit (puns) as an innocuous social diversion that can check dangerous innovation of thought, but implicit elsewhere in the periodical is a warning that excessive or misplaced wit (punning) signals weak or inartificial thinking. Use it sparingly and in appropriate social register.
